chapters.title: Chapter 2: Working Capital and the Cash Conversion Cycle

lessons.title: Working Capital Explained: The Money Stuck in Day-to-Day Operations

children.text: In Chapter 1 you watched cash go round a loop and come back later. Working capital is the name for all the money sitting inside that loop at any moment: goods in the godown, invoices waiting to be paid, minus the bills you have not settled yet. It is the largest single use of cash in most Indian businesses, and unlike a machine or a building, you never see it. There is no asset to point at. There is just money that is somehow not in the bank.

body.text: Working capital is the money your business has already spent but cannot yet use. Every rupee of it was funded by someone: you, your bank, or your suppliers.

children.text: The Definition, and the Version That Actually Helps
The textbook definition is simple arithmetic from the balance sheet.

body.caption: Current means expected to convert to cash, or be paid, within twelve months

children.text: For managing cash day to day, a narrower version is more useful. Strip out cash itself and short-term borrowings, and you are left with the three items you can actually control from your desk: what customers owe you, what sits in stock, and what you owe suppliers.

body.caption: The three levers. Chapter 3 gives one lesson to each of them

body.title: Which way does each item push your cash?

columns.label: Locks cash up
points: Trade receivables: sales billed, money not collected
Inventory: raw material, work in progress, finished goods
Advances paid to suppliers before delivery
Prepaid expenses such as annual insurance or rent deposits
GST input credit stuck in the ledger and not yet used

columns.label: Frees cash up
points: Trade payables: supplier bills not yet paid
Advances received from customers before delivery
Accrued expenses such as salaries payable at month end
Statutory dues sitting until their due date
Credit notes and rebates yet to be settled

body.text: Read the right-hand column again. Every item there is someone else funding your business for free. That is why payment terms, both what you give and what you take, are the cheapest source of finance any business has.

children.text: Konkan Ceramics is a fictional tile manufacturer in Morbi, Gujarat, with annual sales of ₹12 crore and a net margin of 10%, so it earns about ₹1.2 crore a year. Here is where its working capital sits.

body.caption: Konkan Ceramics: operating working capital (₹ crore)

cells: Dealers and builders who have the tiles but have not paid, about 73 days of sales
Clay, glaze, half-finished batches and finished tiles in the godown
Suppliers who have delivered but not been paid. They are funding you
Cash locked in the business at any given moment

stats.label: Locked in working capital
stats.context: Never appears in the bank balance

stats.label: Annual profit
stats.context: The business earns this in a whole year

children.text: Put those last two numbers side by side. Konkan Ceramics has two and a half years of profit permanently parked in tiles and unpaid invoices. That money was earned, borrowed or invested at some point, and it cannot be spent on anything else until the business shrinks or collects better.

body.title: The formula
body.textWithBlank: Working capital is current assets minus ___ liabilities.
body.explanation: Current means due to convert to cash, or be settled, within twelve months. Long-term items such as a five-year term loan sit outside working capital, though their repayments still drain cash.

children.text: Why Growth Sends the Bill Before the Reward

Here is the part that catches managers out. Working capital scales with sales. Sell 50% more tiles and you need roughly 50% more stock in the godown and carry roughly 50% more unpaid invoices. The percentage stays put; the rupees do not.

body.latex: \text{Extra cash needed} = \text{Working capital intensity} \times \text{Increase in sales}
body.caption: Intensity is working capital divided by sales, 25% for Konkan Ceramics

children.text: Suppose Konkan Ceramics wins new dealers and grows from ₹12 crore to ₹18 crore of sales, at the same margins and the same terms.

body.title: Konkan Ceramics: sales vs working capital locked up (₹ crore)

cells: Earned over the year, collected later still
From a bank limit, the promoter, or better terms

body.text: Growth of 50% here consumes ₹1.5 crore of cash and returns ₹0.6 crore of profit in the same year. The business is not doing anything wrong. This is simply what growth costs. Plan the funding before you chase the order, not after the godown is full.

body.title: Price the growth plan
body.prompt: A company has sales of ₹20 crore and working capital of ₹6 crore, so its working capital intensity is 30%. The board approves a plan to add ₹5 crore of sales next year, with no change in credit terms, stock policy or supplier terms. How much extra cash will be locked into working capital, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: 30% of ₹5 crore is ₹1.5 crore. That money must be arranged before the extra sales are delivered, because stock is bought and produced first and the invoices are collected months later. The profit on those sales arrives afterwards and is almost never enough on its own to fund the build-up.

body.title: Is cash in the bank part of working capital?

children.text: Strictly, yes. Cash and bank balances are current assets, so the textbook figure includes them, and short-term borrowings such as a cash credit limit sit in current liabilities.
For management purposes, most finance teams strip both out and track operating working capital instead: receivables plus inventory minus payables. There are two good reasons.
Cash is the result, not the cause.
Including it hides the very thing you are trying to measure, which is how much cash the operations have swallowed.
Borrowings are the funding, not the need.
A larger overdraft makes textbook working capital look smaller, while the underlying problem is unchanged and now costs interest.
When someone quotes a working capital number to you, ask which version it is. The two can differ by crores in the same company.

Working capital intensity is not a fixed law of nature. It depends on who pays whom, and when. A restaurant collects by UPI before the diner leaves and pays its vegetable supplier weekly, so it can run on almost none. A tile maker selling to builders on 75-day credit needs a fortune.

body.label: Titan: 222 days of inventory, 4 days of receivables
body.context: From screener.in consolidated ratios. A jeweller must hold enormous stock, gold and finished designs across hundreds of stores, but customers pay at the counter. So its cash is trapped in inventory, not in invoices. Its reported working capital days are far lower than that inventory figure suggests, because customer advance schemes and gold metal loans fund a large part of the stock. Where cash gets stuck, and who funds it, is specific to each business model.

body.label: screener.in ratios
body.description: Scroll to the Ratios section of any listed company for Debtor Days, Inventory Days, Days Payable and Working Capital Days across ten years.

body.title: Which one releases cash this quarter?
body.question: Konkan Ceramics needs ₹50 lakh of cash within 60 days. Which action releases cash from working capital, rather than consuming more of it?
options: Take up the supplier offer of 8% off for paying all bills immediately instead of in 45 days
Collect the ₹80 lakh of receivables that are already overdue by more than 90 days
Buy three months of clay in advance because prices are expected to rise
Offer dealers an extra 30 days of credit to push volumes up
body.explanation: Collecting overdue money converts an existing current asset straight into cash, with no new spending at all. Paying suppliers early and buying stock in advance both push cash out sooner, and extending dealer credit locks up more. Notice that three of the four options look like good commercial decisions in isolation. Each of them would deepen the cash hole.

body.title: Find ₹1 crore in 60 days
body.scenario: You are on the management team at Konkan Ceramics. The bank limit is fully drawn, a ₹1 crore kiln repair cannot wait, and the promoter will not put in more capital. The CEO asks every function to release cash from working capital within 60 days, without cutting sales.
body.prompt: What would you ask sales, procurement, production and HR to do, and what would you refuse to do?
body.modelAnswer:
Sales and collections
1. Pull the receivables ageing report and chase everything overdue beyond 90 days first, personally, at the dealer-owner level. This is the fastest and cheapest cash in the business.
2. Stop supplying dealers who are more than two invoices behind, until they clear one.
3. Offer a small early payment discount only to the slowest payers, and only for 60 days. Price it against your borrowing cost, not out of relief.
Procurement
4. Freeze all purchases not needed for confirmed orders in the next eight weeks.
5. Ask the two largest suppliers for 15 extra days, offering firm volume commitments in exchange.
Production and stores
6. Identify slow-moving and discontinued designs and clear them, even at a discount. Dead stock is cash that is already spent.
7. Stop building finished stock ahead of forecast demand.
HR
8. Pause non-critical hiring for the quarter and defer discretionary spending such as an offsite, being straight with people about why.
What I would refuse
9. Do not delay statutory dues. TDS, PF and GST carry interest and penalties, and delaying payments to micro and small suppliers beyond the MSMED limit has tax consequences too, which Lesson 3.2 covers.
10. Do not cut the marketing or service spending that keeps the order book alive. Solving a 60-day cash problem by creating a 12-month sales problem is not a solution.

body.title: Work out your own working capital intensity
steps: Take last year's annual sales from the profit and loss statement.
From the balance sheet, note trade receivables, inventories and trade payables.
Calculate receivables plus inventory minus payables. That is operating working capital.
Divide it by sales to get your intensity as a percentage.
Multiply that percentage by next year's planned sales increase. That is the cash your growth plan needs.
Compare that number with the profit the growth is expected to earn.
If the cash need is larger, identify now where the difference comes from: a bank limit, better terms, or a slower growth plan.

cards.definition: Current assets minus current liabilities. The money circulating inside day-to-day operations.
Receivables plus inventory minus payables, excluding cash and borrowings. The version managers can act on.
Working capital divided by sales. Tells you how much cash each rupee of sales locks up.
The extra cash locked up when sales grow. Intensity multiplied by the increase in sales.
Inventory that will not sell at full price. Cash already spent that will only partly come back.
Money collected before delivery. Negative working capital, and the cheapest funding available.

points: Working capital is cash already spent and not yet recoverable: stock in the godown and invoices not yet collected, less what you owe suppliers.
Receivables, inventory and advances paid lock cash up. Payables and customer advances free it.
Konkan Ceramics has ₹3 crore locked up on ₹12 crore of sales, two and a half times its annual profit.
Working capital scales with sales, so growth needs cash upfront and returns profit later. Fund it before the order, not after.
Growing 50% cost ₹1.5 crore of cash and produced ₹0.6 crore of profit in the same year.
Intensity varies hugely by business model. A jeweller is trapped in inventory, a tile maker in receivables, a restaurant in almost nothing.

body.text: Konkan Ceramics is a fictional company. The Titan figures are from screener.in as published at the time of writing and may be restated later. Nothing here is investment advice or a recommendation on any security.
